source.title: Never Go Full Batch (in Stochastic Convex Optimization)
source.authors: I Zaghloul Amir; Y. Carmon; Tomer Koren; Roi Livni

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is supplied.
record.tranche_reason: The paper gives a theoretical lower-bound result on generalization for full-batch first-order methods on stochastic convex losses, directly testing the batch-size/optimization-method aspect of V5 with a different setting and measure than neural-network image or language benchmarks.
record.gate_note: The paper's own results are theoretical bounds for stochastic convex optimization, not empirical deep-network runs. Rows record the theorem's full-batch result and the stated SGD comparison; referenced empirical studies are not this paper's results. The paper states no tested neural-network architecture, model size sweep, or measured network property.
record.test_reason: The paper proves a worst-case oracle-complexity separation in stochastic convex optimization. It does not test V5's image classifiers or language models under fixed epoch budgets, or any other listed version. Its discussion of large-batch neural-network results cites prior work.
record.authors_conclusion: The record captures the main conclusion but needs explicit qualifications: Θ(1/ε⁴) is the worst-case dimension-independent generalization complexity of full-batch methods for the general Lipschitz convex class. Data-independent regularization, noise, or other modifications within this oracle model cannot improve that rate. SGD achieves O(1/ε²); special smooth or strongly convex problem families can admit better full-batch rates.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies theoretical worst-case stochastic convex optimization with an exact empirical full-batch gradient oracle, rather than empirical neural-network training with image or language benchmarks and fixed epoch budgets.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper identifies oracle access and iteration count as central: full-batch methods use the same fixed sample at each query, whereas SGD accesses individual sampled examples. It states a dimension-dependent sample-complexity alternative and that strongly convex or smooth special families can have improved rates.

fits_no_version.finding: For general Lipschitz convex losses, full-batch oracle methods require Ω(1/ε⁴) queries in the worst case for dimension-independent population-risk guarantees, whereas SGD has an O(1/ε²) guarantee. The stated sample-size comparison is Ω(n²) versus O(n) queries.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Access only to aggregate gradients of a fixed sample can impose worse worst-case population-risk oracle complexity than access to individual-example gradients in stochastic convex optimization.

record.problems: The result is a worst-case theoretical lower bound on a constructed convex-loss problem. It does not provide empirical evidence about neural-network classifiers, fixed epoch budgets, architectures, or trained-network measurements. No uncertainty estimate is stated for the theorem's rate.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label held-out accuracy in the same architectures and training recipes.
Test error as network width increases beyond interpolation.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the role of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer performance under limited or broader tuning.
Batch-size effects on image classifiers or language models under fixed epoch budgets, and whether training or recipe adaptations remove those effects.
Dropout's effects on held-out classifier error.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its correlation with generalization gaps.
Test accuracy after removing memorized versus random training examples.

record.verdict_notes: The theoretical separation is relevant background for V5, but differences in system, objective class, and budget prevent a verdict on that version. These untested conditions do not warrant limits_scope.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label memorization or natural-label generalization experiment.
No network-width sweep or interpolation-threshold test.
No convolutional versus fully connected network comparison.

The theoretical result concerns full-batch versus stochastic first-order methods on convex losses, measured in oracle/iteration complexity and expected population risk; it does not test neural-network image or language models, fixed epoch budgets, or the cited recipe adaptations.
No sharpness or other trained-network property is measured.

rows.subject: any full-batch first-order algorithm
rows.operation_detail: Theorem 1 lower-bounds expected population-risk error after at most T full-batch oracle iterations on a constructed 1-Lipschitz convex stochastic optimization problem.
rows.measure: Expected excess true risk, E[F(wS)] − min_w⋆ F(w⋆).
rows.value: at least min_w⋆ F(w⋆) + ε + Ω(min{1 − cε²√T, 0})
rows.note: The authors state this implies at least Ω(1/ε⁴) iterations are needed to obtain less than ε true risk. This is a worst-case theoretical construction, not an empirical batch-size comparison in neural networks.
rows.check: This is a theoretical population-risk lower bound for constructed convex losses, not a measure of V5's fixed-epoch batch-size penalty in image classifiers or language models. The measure is excess risk, but the value includes the optimal-risk term; subtract that term when recording excess risk.

rows.subject: SGD
rows.operation_detail: The paper compares stated stochastic-optimization convergence and generalization rates with its full-batch bound.
rows.measure: Iterations to optimize population risk to within ε.
rows.baseline: full-batch methods require at least Ω(1/ε⁴) iterations or dimension-dependent sample complexity
rows.value: SGD can generalize and optimize population risk to within ε after O(1/ε²) iterations
rows.note: This is a theoretical comparison stated by the paper, not a newly run SGD experiment.
rows.check: The SGD rate is an established theoretical comparator, not a new result of this study. It should not be a standalone study-result row and does not measure any listed version.

rows.subject: full-batch method
rows.operation_detail: Compares iteration/oracle complexity for matching an O(1/√n) test/generalization error rate.
rows.measure: Iterations to achieve stated test/generalization error.
rows.note: The paper also states that in individual gradient calculations, SGD uses at most O(n), while a full-batch method performs Ω(n³).
rows.check: The iteration-complexity comparison concerns worst-case convex optimization, not fixed epoch budgets for the systems in V5. The full-batch lower bound is existential over hard instances, not a requirement for every convex problem.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.condition: Worst-case stochastic convex optimization with full-batch first-order oracle access
reader_labels.reason: The theorem establishes a full-batch iteration lower bound, while the paper's comparison gives SGD a faster stated rate; it does not test the neural-network fixed-epoch setting in V5 (R1–R3).
